This stay continued for nearly one year through multiple adjournments and three judicial recusals, compelling the appellant to approach the Supreme Court.

Ruling: The Supreme Court held that the power to grant interim stay of a bail order under Section 439(2) CrPC or Section 483(3) BNSS can be exercised only in exceptional cases where a very strong prima facie case for cancellation exists, and reasons must be recorded. Ex parte stay of bail orders should not be granted as a standard rule and is permissible only in rare and exceptional circumstances, with an immediate hearing required on continuation. The Court set aside the High Court's stay orders as the ex parte stay was granted without application of mind, continued for one year without hearing the accused, and violated Article 21 liberty protections, while leaving open all merits of the cancellation application.

Key legal principles:
- The power to grant interim stay of an order granting bail under Section 439(2) of the CrPC or Section 483(3) of the BNSS can be exercised only in exceptional cases when a very strong prima facie case of the existence of grounds for cancellation of bail is made out, and the Court must record brief reasons for such conclusion.
- As a normal rule, ex parte stay of an order granting bail should not be granted, and such power can be exercised only in rare and very exceptional cases where the situation demands the passing of such drastic order.
- When an ex parte ad interim stay of an order granting bail is granted, the Court is duty bound to immediately hear the accused on the prayer for continuation of the interim relief and record specific reasons why it concluded that a very rare and exceptional case warranted such drastic order.

Conclusion: Split jurisdiction: IPC governs pre-July acts, BNS governs post-July acts; each period charged under respective law.

Core legal principle: Continuing offenses are governed by the law in force on each date of commission; pre-July 2024 acts under IPC 294A, post-July acts under BNS 297.

question: Summarize the judgment involving BNSS_2023_SEC_483, IPC_1860_SEC_439, PMLA_SEC_045 and state the core ruling.
assistant_reply:
Facts: Parvinder Singh Khurana was arrested on 20 January 2023 by the Enforcement Directorate in a money laundering case under the PMLA, though he was not initially named as an accused in the ECIR or first complaint. After his first bail application was rejected on 10 March 2023, a supplementary complaint was filed naming him as an accused, and he was granted regular bail by the Special Court on 17 June 2023 after satisfying Section 45(1)(ii) of the PMLA. The Directorate filed an application for cancellation of bail under Section 439(2) CrPC before the Delhi High Court on 21 June 2023, and on 23 June 2023, a Single Judge granted an ex parte stay of the bail order without hearing the appellant or recording reasons. This stay continued for nearly one year through multiple adjournments and three judicial recusals, compelling the appellant to approach the Supreme Court.

Ruling: The Supreme Court held that the power to grant interim stay of a bail order under Section 439(2) CrPC or Section 483(3) BNSS can be exercised only in exceptional cases where a very strong prima facie case for cancellation exists, and reasons must be recorded. Ex parte stay of bail orders should not be granted as a standard rule and is permissible only in rare and exceptional circumstances, with an immediate hearing required on continuation. The Court set aside the High Court's stay orders as the ex parte stay was granted without application of mind, continued for one year without hearing the accused, and violated Article 21 liberty protections, while leaving open all merits of the cancellation application.

Key legal principles:

- As a normal rule, ex parte stay of an order granting bail should not be granted, and such power can be exercised only in rare and very exceptional cases where the situation demands the passing of such drastic order.
- When an ex parte ad interim stay of an order granting bail is granted, the Court is duty bound to immediately hear the accused on the prayer for continuation of the interim relief and record specific reasons why it concluded that a very rare and exceptional case warranted such drastic order.

question: Distinguish Section 238 from Section 58 (Concealing design to commit offence) in terms of temporal application and the nature of the conduct protected against.
assistant_reply:
Section 58 applies to concealing a design to commit an offence that is yet to be committed (pre-offence conduct), while Section 238 applies to causing disappearance of evidence or giving false information after an offence has already been committed (post-offence conduct). Section 58 is preventive, targeting interference with the prevention of future crimes, while Section 238 is remedial, targeting interference with the investigation and prosecution of past crimes. The temporal distinction is crucial: ongoing concealment that spans both phases may require careful analysis, but Section 58 requires intent to facilitate the future offence, while Section 238 requires intent to screen the offender from punishment for the completed offence.

Legal Analysis (IRAC):
Issue: How do Sections 58 and 238 differ in their temporal application?
Rule: Section 58 applies to concealing a design to commit an offence (future); Section 238 applies to screening an offender after an offence has been committed (past).
Application: Section 58 is preventive, punishing interference with crime prevention. Section 238 is remedial, punishing interference with justice administration. The same act of concealing might violate Section 58 if done before the offence to facilitate it, or Section 238 if done after to protect the offender. The intent differs: facilitating commission vs screening from punishment.
Conclusion: The sections are temporally distinct: Section 58 is pre-offence, Section 238 is post-offence.

Core legal principle: Section 58 applies to pre-offence concealment of design; Section 238 applies to post-offence screening from punishment.

question: If the manufacturer was producing the dies on June 20, 2024, which substantive law applies and what is the transitional framework for proceedings initiated after BNS commencement for pre-BNS acts?

question: How does Section 310 relate to Section 313 (Punishment for belonging to gang of robbers), and what distinguishes the offense of dacoity from belonging to a gang of robbers under the BNS?
assistant_reply:
Sections 310 and 313 address different aspects of organized property crime. Section 310 defines dacoity as the actual commission or attempt to commit robbery by five or more persons acting conjointly. It is an offense of execution, punishing the act of collective robbery. Section 313 punishes belonging to a gang of persons associated for the purpose of habitually committing theft or robbery, where the gang is not a gang of dacoits. It is an offense of membership, punishing the association for habitual criminality. The distinction is that dacoity requires the specific act of robbery by five persons together, while Section 313 requires membership in a gang that habitually commits theft or robbery, which may involve fewer than five persons or may not involve the immediate commission of robbery by the entire group. Dacoity is punishable with life or up to ten years, while belonging to a gang of robbers is punishable with up to seven years.

Legal Analysis (IRAC):
Issue: What distinguishes dacoity under Section 310 from belonging to a gang of robbers under Section 313?
Rule: Section 310 requires five or more persons conjointly committing robbery. Section 313 requires belonging to a gang associated for habitually committing theft or robbery, not being a gang of dacoits.
Application: The critical difference is the nature of the criminal activity. Dacoity is a specific event or attempt involving five persons in a robbery. Belonging to a gang of robbers is a continuing status offense based on association for habitual criminality. A gang of robbers under Section 313 might consist of four persons who habitually commit theft, or it might be a larger group where not all participate in each crime. Dacoity is a more serious offense with higher punishment because it involves the immediate danger of collective violence during robbery.
Conclusion: Section 310 addresses the execution of collective robbery, while Section 313 addresses membership in a criminal association for habitual theft or robbery.

Core legal principle: Dacoity is the commission of robbery by five persons conjointly, while Section 313 punishes membership in a gang habitually committing theft or robbery.

question: Summarize the judgment involving IPC_1860_SEC_376, IPC_1860_SEC_376-E, IPC_1860_SEC_53 and state the core ruling.
assistant_reply:
Facts: The petitioners—Mohd. Salim Mohd. Kudus Ansari, Mohd. Kasim Mohd Hasim Shaikh, and Vijay Jadhav—were convicted in two simultaneous rape trials (Sessions Cases 914/2013 and 846/2013). After conviction in the first case on 20 March 2014, the prosecution applied under Section 211(7) Cr.P.C. to frame charges under Section 376-E IPC for repeat offenders. The petitioners challenged the constitutional validity of Section 376-E before the Bombay High Court, seeking to quash the charge and stay proceedings. The trial continued and resulted in death sentences under Section 376-E, leading to the filing of Writ Petition No. 527 of 2018 by Vijay Jadhav.

Ruling: The Bombay High Court upheld the constitutional validity of Section 376-E IPC, rejecting challenges under Articles 14 and 21. The Court held that 'imprisonment for life which shall mean imprisonment for the remainder of that person's natural life' does not create a new punishment category but falls within Section 53 IPC read with Section 45 IPC, as clarified by the Constitution Bench in V. Sriharan. The Court found no denial of constitutional remission powers under Articles 72 and 161, no mandatory death sentence (as alternative punishment of life imprisonment exists), and no violation of proportionality principles. The petitions were dismissed.

Key legal principles:
- Imprisonment for life which shall mean imprisonment for the remainder of that person's natural life does not create a new category of punishment but falls within the purview of Section 53 of the Indian Penal Code read with Section 45 thereof.
- The constitutional powers of remission under Articles 72 and 161 of the Constitution remain untouched and available to a convict sentenced under Section 376-E of the Indian Penal Code.
- Statutory powers of remission under Sections 432 and 433 of the Code of Criminal Procedure are not available during the period of life imprisonment specified by the Court, but revive automatically once that period is undergone.
